title: General Survey: First Impressions and Initial Assessment
learning_goal: Learners will identify and correctly prioritize observations during a general survey, including patient appearance, behavior, and cognitive status, and select appropriate follow-up actions based on those findings.
target_audience: Nursing students in foundational clinical assessment coursework
visual_style: 2D semi-flat limited animation with dynamic but constrained movement. Characters express emotion through head turns, nods, subtle posture shifts, and facial expressions. Mouth movement suggests speech without phoneme-level lip sync. Consistent character designs and color palette across all clips.

decision_points.question_text: Caleb has just entered the room and begun his first encounter with Diane. She is pale, leaning forward, and reports shortness of breath and fatigue. What should Caleb do first as part of his general survey?

choices.text: Pause and complete a deliberate visual observation of Diane, noting her skin color, posture, and any signs of respiratory effort before proceeding.
Start with the medical history review so the assessment follows a structured order and no information is missed.
choices.misconception: Learners may believe that following a fixed documentation sequence is the priority, but the general survey begins with observation before history-taking. Pallor and forward-leaning posture in a patient reporting shortness of breath are immediate visual cues that must be noted first.

choices.text: Note that Diane is sitting forward but assume it is a comfort preference, and begin asking intake questions right away.
choices.misconception: Learners may interpret a forward-leaning posture as simply a patient positioning choice, but this posture is a known sign of respiratory distress. A nurse conducting a general survey must recognize and follow up on behavioral and postural cues, not dismiss them.

decision_points.question_text: Diane correctly states her name, location, and the approximate time of day, but says she does not know what day it is. How should Caleb interpret and respond to this finding?

choices.text: Ask Diane a follow-up question, such as why she came to the hospital, to help clarify her overall level of orientation before making a documentation decision.
Document Diane as alert and oriented times four because she answered three of the four questions correctly and the missed date is likely not meaningful.
choices.misconception: Learners may think that nearly correct answers justify a full orientation score, but orientation must be documented accurately based on what the patient actually demonstrated. A follow-up question is the appropriate step before finalizing the assessment.

choices.text: Document Diane as alert and oriented times two because she could not identify the date, and flag this as a potential change in cognition.
choices.misconception: Learners may over-correct by treating a missed date as a significant cognitive deficit without considering that hospitalized patients commonly lose track of dates due to disrupted routines. The chapter notes this explicitly and recommends a follow-up question rather than an immediate downgrade of orientation status.
